t: How To Love Being A Teacher
q: More is being asked of us now than at any time in my 25 years of teaching. Stress is at an all-time high.
And yet, there is a small band of teachers who have figured out how to fight back.
They’ve figured out how to love being a teacher. (And not just try to convince themselves they do.)

The book is a culmination of my career-long quest for the single most effective and fulfilling teaching approach in existence—and not just in the classroom, but from the moment you arrive on campus until you leave for the day.
I’ve taken the traits, qualities, and practices of the happiest and most effective teachers on Earth and condensed them into 11 habits any teacher can apply and experience dramatic results.
It was important to me not just to tell you that a particular method or strategy is effective, but show you exactly why it’s effective and how you can apply it in your own classroom.

q: It is this: Many victims are unsure if they’re actually being bullied.
You see, bullies are good at making you think that they’re really your friend.
This underscores the importance of defining for your students—through modeling, playacting, and role-playing—what bullying looks like.
It’s a very simple test, but it’s 100% accurate in determining who is and isn’t a bully.
But what it does do is give the victim a surefire way to know if they’re being bullied. Because, if the person being asked doesn’t stop, then by definition, they’re a bully.
Furthermore, when “please stop” becomes the culture of your classroom or school it can virtually wipe out bullying behavior.
x: As a follow-up to an earlier comprehensive anti-bullying guide, Linsin addresses a specific gap.
Making "please stop" a known classroom culture puts all potential bullies on notice and helps borderline offenders recognize their own behavior.
Proposed test: the victim specifically asks the other student to stop a named behavior — if they don't stop, they are by definition a bully.
This test doesn't replace teacher intervention against a determined bully but gives victims clarity and a concrete tool.

t: Can’t Need It, Gotta Want It
q: My message today is simple. We cannot afford to need this kind of recognition, or any kind of recognition.

Too many teachers needlessly brutalize themselves by needing recognition or affirmation for their work. Too many teachers feel they have no autonomy in their work because they enslave themselves to externalism. In their need for recognition, they inevitably get demolished by anti-recognition.

The affirmation, after all, isn't about the kids — it's about us. It's us saying, “I've got this insatiable need for affirmation, and I need my students or my principal to fulfill it.” I'm dumbfounded by how many teachers fool themselves into thinking they love their students when actually they love the way their students make them feel.

And the final step is, instead of needing the affirmation, we need to want the results. I didn't teach Caleb hoping he'd one day call me (see the end of this post), but I certainly taught Caleb hoping his life would turn out well and that my English Language Arts class would help.

But it's exactly the opposite — I'm telling you that the only way to care enough is by detaching your self-worth; I'm saying that you don't really care, cleanly, until you've rid yourself of needing affirmation and filled yourself up with the drive to harvest the fruits that affirmation points to. That's where the truly courageous teachers live and do their work.
x: He claims the need for recognition sets teachers up to be demolished by its opposite, since a single student's contempt becomes devastating to anyone who depends on student approval.
He claims the need for recognition sets teachers up to be demolished by its opposite, since a single student's contempt becomes devastating to anyone who depends on student approval.
His most pointed diagnosis is that many teachers who believe they love their students actually love the way their students make them feel.
Stuart's core distinction is between needing affirmation and wanting results.
Detaching self-worth from the work, he concludes, is not caring less but the precondition of caring cleanly and teaching courageously.

t: How to Handle A Student Who Yells At You
q: But then, out of the blue, a student stood up and accused her of favoring one team over another.
The instant you recognize—or think you recognize—a student becoming angry, your singular goal is to calm them down and avoid confrontation.

Instead, stay cool and relaxed, pretend it’s no big deal, and say “It’s okay. I understand what you’re saying. I can see how you might feel that way. I promise I’ll fix it, but let’s finish the game first.
You are under no obligation to explain yourself or your decisions to any student who speaks to you or approaches you disrespectfully —nor should you.

Any incident of brazen or continued disrespect should be met with your strongest consequence—which may include an extended time-out for elementary students or detention for high school students—plus a notification of parents.
As counterintuitive as it may seem, the less contact you have with the offending student, the less likely a similar incident will happen in the future.
x: Prompted by a reader's account of a student who suddenly yelled and accused her of favoritism during a game, Linsin lays out a four-step response for de-escalating confrontational outbursts.
After things calm down, clarify the relevant rule to the whole class rather than over-explaining to the individual student.
In the moment, delay engaging with an angry student's accusations rather than defending yourself directly — promise to "fix it" later and move on.

Brazen disrespect warrants skipping the warning stage and may include parent notification or administrator referral for serious incidents.
Minimizing direct contact with the offending student afterward.

q: The phrase “in a moment” keeps students from moving on while you’re giving directions.
It bridges the gap between knowing what to do and doing it with speed, accuracy, and confidence.
Because once you say ‘go,’ you’re handing responsibility in total over to them—with very reluctant additional support from you.
A final pause of 15-20 seconds will cause students to visualize themselves successfully doing whatever you want them to do.
This simple two-part strategy of giving directions— in a moment and when I say go —can turn distracted, bored, and daydreaming students into active and tenacious listeners.
x: Combined with the earlier "in a moment" phrase, the two-part strategy is meant to turn distracted or daydreaming students into active listeners.
The phrase "when I say go," said right before releasing students to a task, bridges the gap between understanding directions and executing with speed and confidence.
Pause for final clarifying questions before giving the "go" signal — once said, responsibility shifts entirely to students.
A deliberate 15-20 second pause before saying "go" causes students to mentally visualize success, building useful suspense.

t: What is the Role of Education?
q: Would we not be better served to start with why we want to educate humans and then build a curriculum to suit that need?
What if we designed our education systems to build better humans by focusing on an adaptable set of skills? The kind of skills that lead to self-directed learning over the course of a lifetime.

Research – in a world where every book in history will one day be cataloged by Google; where any fact can be found in seconds; where any calculation can be performed automatically… the key skill will not be memorizing information, but accessing it. Organizing it. Interpreting it.

Children (and adults for that matter) don't need to be forced to learn topics, they simply need to be exposed to enough topics to find one they can get lost in. And if they don't learn the history of the industrial revolution, oh well!
It means that every child should be named captain of at least one team — not given a trophy, but given responsibility and encouragement to lead. Every child should be taught to make their own rules.
The best we can hope, and perhaps all we could ever hope from a great education: Show people their own capacity, and give them the confidence and courage to lead.
There is no test that will gauge a person's ability to be a good human and protect the world for future generations. Why do we pretend that there is?
x: He proposes instead to design from principles that build capable, self-directed humans.
He proposes instead to design from principles that build capable, self-directed humans.
His six principles favor adaptable, self-directed learning skills over subject coverage, especially research as access and interpretation rather than memorization.
Guest post by Barrett Brooks, introduced by Dave Stuart Jr., asking what education is actually for before anyone commits to systems like the Common Core or universal college.
Leadership is treated as an educational outcome: every child should be given real responsibility and taught to define personal values and communicate them.
His thesis is that education should show people their own capacity and give them the courage to lead, and that no test can measure that.
He closes by contrasting a principle-centered system with a test-centered one, arguing that no test gauges a person's ability to be a good human.

q: As soon as your students think they understand what you’re asking of them, they mentally check out.
In response, it’s common for teachers to increase the volume of their voice in an effort to cut through the fog.
A better way to handle it is to utter three simple words before giving directions.
The phrase is: “In a moment.” As in, “In a moment, we’re going to begin writing a response to the day’s reading.
It keeps students from moving on mentally or physically until you’ve finished giving every last direction.
The most effective teachers use the phrase up to a dozen times a day.
Eventually, active listening will become Pavlovian in response.
x: Linsin diagnoses a common frustration: students who mentally check out and begin moving as soon as they think they understand directions, causing the teacher to lose them before finishing critical details.
